text: New project: an open-data tide predictor for small harbors. Goal: publishable predictions for any NOAA station, runnable on a laptop. Working name: marlin.
speaker: dana

text: Two candidate approaches on the table: classical harmonic analysis (fit named tidal constituents, predict by superposition) versus training a small neural net on station history.
speaker: kim

text: Argument for the neural net: no oceanography knowledge needed, just data. Argument against: it's a black box, and we can't explain a bad prediction to a harbormaster.
speaker: dana

text: DECISION: we go with classical harmonic analysis, 37 named constituents (M2, S2, N2, K1, O1 and the rest of the standard set). Explainable, deterministic, a century of literature behind it. The neural net is parked, not rejected — revisit only if harmonic residuals stay above 10 cm.
speaker: kim

text: Agreed. The deal is: explainability over novelty, and we only add machine learning where the classical method measurably fails. That's the way we work on this one.
speaker: dana

text: Scaffolded the repo: fetch/ pulls NOAA CO-OPS water-level history, fit/ does the least-squares constituent fit, predict/ superposes constituents forward. Self-tests green on synthetic sine data.
speaker: agent

text: First real fit: Seattle station 9447130, one year of hourly data. M2 amplitude comes out 1.07 m, phase 10.3 degrees — matches NOAA's published harmonic constants to two decimals. The method works.
speaker: agent

text: Note for later: the constituent fit needs at least 369 days of data to separate S2 from K2 (the Rayleigh criterion). Shorter records silently alias them. Added a hard check in fit/.
speaker: agent

text: Kim asks: where do the fitted constants live? Right now each fit dumps JSON next to the script, which is a mess.
speaker: kim

text: Moved all fitted calibration constants to config/constituents.yaml — one file, keyed by station id, amplitudes in meters and phases in degrees, with the fit date and record length recorded per station. fetch/ and predict/ both read from there now. Old JSON dumps deleted.
speaker: agent

text: Good. Single source of truth for calibration from now on: config/constituents.yaml. Nothing else stores constants.
speaker: dana

text: Built scripts/backtest.py: takes a station id and a date range, predicts from the fitted constituents, pulls the actual observed water levels, and reports RMS error and worst-hour error. This is our honesty check — predictions mean nothing without it.
speaker: agent

text: Backtest on Seattle 9447130, May 2026: RMS error 6.2 cm, worst hour 18 cm during a storm surge (expected — harmonics don't model weather). Under the 10 cm bar. The classical method is holding.
speaker: agent

text: Adding a second station for validation: La Jolla, station 9410230. Fit completed from 400 days of hourly data, constants written to config/constituents.yaml.
speaker: agent

text: Problem: La Jolla backtest shows a constant offset — every prediction is about 0.8 m low. RMS error 81 cm. Something systematic, not noise.
speaker: kim

text: Found it: a datum mismatch. Our fetch pulled observations referenced to MLLW (mean lower low water) but the fit assumed NAVD88. The 0.8 m is exactly the MLLW-to-NAVD88 offset at that station. It's not the physics, it's the reference frame.
speaker: agent

text: Fix: fetch/ now requests everything in MLLW explicitly, and config/constituents.yaml records the datum per station. Never trust a water level without its datum — that's the lesson. Seattle refit for consistency.
speaker: agent

text: Re-ran the La Jolla backtest after the datum fix for the first week of June: RMS down from 81 cm to 5.9 cm. The offset is gone. Still need the full-month validation run to call it closed.
speaker: agent

text: Current stride: validating the datum fix on La Jolla 9410230 across the whole of May 2026 — full-month backtest, then write the validation note. After that, the next station on the list is Galveston.
speaker: dana

text: Reminder from Kim: whatever we publish, the README claims only what the backtests show — per-station RMS numbers with dates, no marketing. Same bar we set on day one.
speaker: kim
